summary: Registers the MIME sub-type application/xv+xml, intended as a media descriptor for XHTML+Voice multimodal language documents. The document is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A label for a document that mixes a web page with voice features, so programs know what it is.

questions: what does application/xv+xml media type mean
can a browser without voice support display xhtml+voice
why do documents need media types
subtitle: Media type identifier for multimodal documents mixing web pages and voice

tldr.problem: XHTML+Voice is a language that mixes web page markup with voice interaction commands, allowing both visual and voice-based user interaction in a single document. There was no standard MIME type to label these documents when served over the web.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC registers the MIME media type application/xv+xml as the standard label for XHTML+Voice documents, following the IANA registration process and the rules for XML-based media types.
tldr.outcome: Web servers and browsers can now correctly identify XHTML+Voice documents and invoke the appropriate parser and voice rendering engine to handle both the visual and voice components.

today: RFC 4374 registers application/xv+xml as the MIME type for XHTML+Voice documents. XHTML+Voice itself is maintained by the VoiceXML Forum and is used in multimodal applications that blend web and voice interfaces, though widespread adoption has been limited.

sections.title: XHTML+Voice: Web Pages With Voice
sections.content:
XHTML+Voice is an extension of XHTML that adds voice interaction capabilities. It combines standard XHTML markup (the language of web pages) with a subset of VoiceXML (a language for voice-based interactions) and XML Events (a standard way to attach event handlers to document elements). This lets a single document provide both a visual interface and a voice interface.

For example, a document might have a text input field for a user to type a search query, but also voice commands so the user can say the search term. The same document can be displayed visually on a screen and understood by a voice browser that reads the page aloud and accepts spoken input.

XHTML+Voice is specified by the VoiceXML Forum as a modularized host language conformant with XHTML Modularization. It uses the same W3C standards as regular XHTML, ensuring broad compatibility. The document type is maintained and published by the VoiceXML Forum.
sections.plainLanguage: A document type that puts web page instructions and voice instructions in the same file, so a device with a screen and a microphone can show you a page and let you talk to it.

sections.title: Why a Media Type Was Needed
sections.content:
When a web server sends a document to a browser, it includes a MIME media type header that describes what kind of document it is. The media type tells the browser whether it is receiving an HTML page (text/html), a JPEG image (image/jpeg), a PDF (application/pdf), or something else. The browser uses this label to decide which rendering engine to use.

Without a standard media type, an XHTML+Voice document served by a web server would need to be labeled as generic application/xml or application/xhtml+xml, which would not indicate that voice capabilities are present. An XHTML+Voice-capable browser would have to guess, based on the file extension or document structure, that it should invoke the voice engine.

By registering a dedicated MIME type, XHTML+Voice documents can be unambiguously identified in transit. Servers can correctly label them, and multimodal browsers know immediately that both visual and voice rendering capabilities are needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Without a label, a document just says 'I am some XML.' With a real label, it says 'I am an XHTML+Voice page, with web visual stuff and voice stuff,' so the right program knows how to open it.

sections.title: MIME Type Registration
sections.content:
This RFC registers the MIME media type application/xv+xml according to the IANA process defined in RFC 3023. The registration specifies:

Required parameters: none. Every application/xv+xml document is processed the same way.

Optional parameters: the charset parameter works the same way as for application/xml, allowing the document to specify the character encoding (such as UTF-8).

Encoding considerations: XHTML+Voice follows the same encoding rules as XML, defined in RFC 3023.

Interoperability: Because XHTML+Voice uses W3C standard modules and identifies its extensions by XML namespace, a standard XML processor that does not know about voice elements can still parse and render the XHTML portions without the voice features. This namespace-based approach ensures backward compatibility. A browser without voice capabilities can display the XHTML content as a regular web page.

File extensions: common file extensions include .mxml, .xhvml, .xvml, and .xvm, though the media type is the authoritative label.

Intended usage: Limited use. XHTML+Voice is designed for specific multimodal applications rather than universal web use.
sections.plainLanguage: The official registration says: when you see the label application/xv+xml, it is an XHTML+Voice document. You can optionally say what character set it uses. It follows XML encoding rules.

sections.title: Identifying XHTML+Voice Documents
sections.content:
An XHTML+Voice document is XML, so it optionally begins with an XML declaration like <?xml version='1.0'?>. It must have a DOCTYPE declaration specifying the XHTML+Voice document type. For XHTML+Voice 1.2, the DOCTYPE is:

<!DOCTYPE html PUBLIC "-//VoiceXML Forum//DTD XHTML+Voice 1.2//EN" "http://www.voicexml.org/specs/multimodal/x+v/12/dtd/xhtml+voice12.dtd">

Like all XHTML documents, the root element is <html>, which appears near the top of the file. The presence of this DOCTYPE, together with voice elements from the VoiceXML namespace, uniquely identifies the document as XHTML+Voice.
sections.plainLanguage: An XHTML+Voice file starts with an XML declaration and a DOCTYPE that says 'I am XHTML+Voice 1.2,' then the HTML content begins with <html>.

sections.title: Security and Interoperability
sections.content:
XHTML+Voice inherits security considerations from both XHTML and VoiceXML. XHTML security includes the usual web risks: interpreting hyperlinks and form submissions, and executing embedded scripts. These are the same risks present in ordinary web pages.

VoiceXML security adds voice-specific concerns: voice dialogs and speech recognition, which can be triggered by both the XHTML and VoiceXML markup. A malicious document could use voice commands to execute unintended actions.

XML Events allow attaching handlers to any node in the document. These handlers can trigger voice dialogs or scripts, either in the same document or by loading external code. This power requires careful content security policies.

Interoperability is strong because XHTML+Voice is built on W3C standards. Browsers with namespace support can render the XHTML portions of an XHTML+Voice document as regular HTML, ignoring the voice elements if voice rendering is not available. This graceful degradation means the document is not entirely useless in non-multimodal browsers.
sections.plainLanguage: XHTML+Voice has the same risks as web pages plus voice risks: injected commands, script execution, and event handlers. But it degrades gracefully—a regular browser can show the visual part without voice.
